This is a direct consequence of the fact that floating-point numbers are spaced non-uniformly along the real line, with gaps that grow as magnitude grows, so the order in which values are combined determines which values get rounded away and which survive. Mathematically, real-number addition is associative, but floating-point addition is only an approximation to it, and that approximation depends on grouping.

This has significant consequences for large matrix multiplications, which involve computing sums of many products, one per matrix element in the reduction dimension. On modern hardware, these sums are not computed in a fixed, deterministic order. GPUs and multi-core CPUs parallelize the reduction across many threads, warps, or vector lanes, splitting the terms into partial sums that are computed independently and then combined. The number of partial groups, their sizes, and the order in which they are merged can vary depending on the number of threads scheduled, the tiling strategy chosen by a kernel, the specific hardware architecture, the compiler, or even runtime factors like thread scheduling and occupancy. Because floating-point addition is not associative, different reduction orders produce different rounding patterns and therefore slightly different final results, even though they are mathematically computing the same sum.

For a single addition this difference is negligible, but matrix multiplications aggregate millions or billions of such additions across an entire computation graph, and small discrepancies can accumulate or get amplified by subsequent operations, especially in deep neural networks where results feed into further matrix multiplications, nonlinearities, and normalization layers. This means that running the same matrix multiplication twice, on different GPUs, with a different batch size, thread configuration, or library version, can yield results that are not bit-for-bit identical, even though they should be equal in exact arithmetic. This complicates reproducibility in scientific computing and machine learning, where researchers may want deterministic, exactly repeatable results for debugging, auditing, or verifying training runs. To obtain such determinism, practitioners often must sacrifice performance by forcing fixed reduction orders or using specialized deterministic algorithms, since fully exploiting parallel hardware inherently introduces variability in floating-point summation order.

# Floating-Point Arithmetic and Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware deviates from the mathematical properties we expect from real numbers. One of the most consequential deviations is that addition is not associative, meaning that (a + b) + c does not necessarily equal a + (b + c) when implemented in standard floating-point formats like IEEE 754.

This non-associativity stems from the finite precision inherent in floating-point representation. Every number is stored with a limited number of significant digits, and when two numbers of vastly different magnitudes are added together, the smaller value can be completely lost due to rounding. Consider adding a very large number to a very small number and then to another moderately sized value. Depending on the order in which these operations occur, different intermediate values get rounded at different stages, leading to different final results.

The IEEE 754 standard specifies that each operation should produce a result rounded to the nearest representable value. This rounding introduces error, and the cumulative effect of these errors depends critically on the sequence of operations. If we compute (a + b) + c, the intermediate result of a + b gets rounded first, and then that rounded result is added to c and rounded again. If we instead compute a + (b + c), we get a different sequence of rounding events, and thus a different final answer.

This becomes particularly problematic when performing large matrix multiplications, where we must sum many products together to compute each element of the result matrix. A matrix multiplication computing the dot product of two vectors requires summing the products of corresponding elements. The order in which these partial products are accumulated directly affects the final result due to floating-point rounding errors.

Different reduction orders—different ways of grouping and summing the partial products—will produce observably different results. For instance, summing from the smallest partial products to the largest generally produces different results than summing from largest to smallest or using a tree-like reduction pattern. In parallel computing environments, where different processor cores or GPUs might perform reductions in different orders to optimize performance, this becomes a serious concern.

The practical consequence is that reproducing numerical results from matrix multiplications across different hardware, different library implementations, or even different run configurations becomes extremely difficult. What appears to be deterministic computation on paper becomes genuinely non-deterministic in practice. A simulation that produces consistent results on one system may yield slightly different answers when run on another architecture or even when using different optimization flags on the same machine. This non-reproducibility is not a bug but an intrinsic feature of floating-point computation, necessitating careful consideration in scientific computing, machine learning, and any domain requiring numerical consistency and validation.

When two such numbers are added, the exact mathematical sum usually requires more significand bits than the format provides, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. That rounding is the source of non-associativity. Addition itself is correctly rounded and commutative, but rounding is applied after each individual operation, so a different grouping of the same terms means a different sequence of intermediate roundings, and the accumulated errors differ. The classic illustration uses a large value and two small ones: in IEEE 754 double precision, (1 + 2⁻⁵³) + 2⁻⁵³ evaluates to exactly 1, because each small addend is individually lost to rounding, while 1 + (2⁻⁵³ + 2⁻⁵³) equals 1 + 2⁻⁵² which is representable and therefore distinct. Catastrophic cancellation makes the effect worse: if a partial sum grows large and later terms nearly cancel it, the surviving digits are dominated by whatever information was already discarded. Nothing about this is a hardware defect; a machine that produced associative addition would either need unbounded precision or would have to abandon correct rounding.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a huge collection of dot products, and a dot product is a reduction — precisely the operation whose result depends on grouping. A high-performance implementation never sums a length-k dot product left to right. It blocks the k dimension for cache reuse, keeps several independent accumulators in vector registers to hide the latency of the fused multiply-add pipeline, splits k across threads or across GPU warps and combines partial results in a tree, and may switch among differently tuned kernels depending on matrix shape, alignment, or available instruction set. Each of these choices fixes a particular reduction order. Change the number of threads, the tile size, the vector width, the GPU's occupancy, or the library version, and the reduction order changes with it — so the numerical result changes in the last few bits even though the algorithm is nominally identical and every operation is correctly rounded.

The practical consequences are that bitwise-identical output cannot be assumed across machines, thread counts, or runs when atomics or dynamic scheduling make the order itself nondeterministic. Small discrepancies can then be amplified by iterative or chaotic downstream computation, which is why comparisons should use tolerances rather than equality, why regression tests on neural network training are fragile, and why libraries advertise optional deterministic or "reproducible" modes that pin the reduction order, use fixed-point or extended-precision accumulators, or apply compensated summation, generally at some cost in speed.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity in Matrix Computation

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware does not obey the associative property due to the finite precision with which numbers are represented and computed. When we add three numbers a, b, and c, the result of (a + b) + c is generally not identical to a + (b + c), even though these expressions are mathematically equivalent. This deviation emerges from the way computers handle rounding errors inherent to floating-point representation.

Every floating-point number is stored with a limited number of bits, typically 53 bits for the mantissa in double-precision format. When two floating-point numbers are added, the result may have more significant digits than can be represented, forcing the hardware to round the result to fit within the available precision. The direction and magnitude of this rounding depend on the specific values being added and the rounding mode selected. Consequently, when different orderings of addition operations are performed, different rounding errors accumulate, leading to different final results.

Consider adding four numbers where some are much larger than others. If we add a very large number to a very small number first, the small number's contribution may be completely lost due to rounding, as the result rounds back to the large number. However, if we first add the small numbers together and then add their sum to the large number, we might preserve more precision from the smaller values. This phenomenon is called catastrophic cancellation in the context of subtraction and loss of significance for addition.

Matrix multiplication involves computing inner products, which are themselves large reduction operations summing many terms. When executing matrix multiplication on parallel hardware or with different algorithmic decompositions, the order in which partial products are summed changes. One implementation might sum results row by row, another column by column, and a third might use a tree-structured reduction. Each ordering produces a distinct sequence of rounding errors, resulting in different final values for matrix elements.

This non-associativity severely impacts reproducibility in scientific computing. Running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, with different compiler optimizations, or even with different thread scheduling on the same hardware can produce slightly different numerical results. For some applications, these differences are negligible, but in iterative algorithms or when results are compared for exact equality rather than approximate equivalence, this variability becomes problematic.

Researchers addressing this issue employ techniques such as higher-precision accumulation buffers, enforcing deterministic reduction orders across all runs, or using compensated summation algorithms like Kahan summation, which tracks rounding errors and attempts to correct them in subsequent operations. These approaches trade computational cost or memory usage for improved reproducibility and numerical stability in large-scale matrix computations.

Ensuring bitwise reproducibility therefore often requires fixing the reduction order explicitly, using deterministic algorithms provided by libraries, or accepting that only approximate numerical agreement, not exact bit-for-bit equality, is achievable across different hardware configurations or parallelization strategies.

Floating-point addition fails to be associative because computers represent real numbers with a fixed, finite number of significant bits, typically following the IEEE 754 standard. Each arithmetic operation produces a result that must be rounded to fit back into this limited representation. When you add two floating-point numbers, the exact mathematical sum may require more precision than the format allows, so the hardware rounds the result to the nearest representable value. This rounding introduces a small error at every step. Crucially, the amount and direction of this error depends on the relative magnitudes of the two numbers being added at that particular moment. If you change the order in which numbers are summed, you change the intermediate values being added together at each step, which changes when and how rounding errors occur, and thus changes the final accumulated result. Mathematically, (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) are equal for real numbers, but for floating-point numbers they can differ because the rounding applied after computing a + b is not the same as the rounding applied after computing b + c.

This has direct consequences for large matrix multiplications, which fundamentally rely on computing sums of many products, one for each entry along the shared dimension of the two matrices. The mathematical definition of matrix multiplication does not specify an order for this summation, but any concrete implementation must choose one. On modern hardware, the order of these additions is influenced by many factors: the number of threads used, how work is partitioned and scheduled across cores, whether the computation runs on a CPU or GPU, the specific BLAS library or kernel implementation, tiling and blocking strategies chosen for cache efficiency, and even nondeterministic scheduling of parallel reductions where partial sums from different processing units are combined in whatever order they happen to complete. Because different hardware configurations, library versions, thread counts, or even repeated runs on the same machine can produce different reduction orders, the tiny rounding discrepancies introduced at each addition step propagate differently, leading to final results that differ in the last few bits of precision.

For a single matrix multiplication, these differences are usually negligible, appearing only in the least significant digits. However, in large-scale computations such as deep neural network training, where millions of matrix multiplications are chained together and their outputs feed into subsequent operations, these small discrepancies can compound over many layers and iterations. This makes it difficult to obtain bit-for-bit identical results when running the same model on different hardware, different parallelization strategies, or even the same hardware with a different number of threads, which poses real challenges for debugging, verification, and scientific reproducibility.

# The Problem of Floating-Point Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern computers deviates from the mathematical properties we expect from real numbers. One of the most consequential deviations is that addition is not associative: computing (a + b) + c does not necessarily yield the same result as a + (b + c). This seemingly abstract mathematical property becomes a serious practical concern when performing large numerical computations, particularly matrix multiplications where billions of additions accumulate intermediate results.

The root cause lies in how floating-point numbers are represented and combined. Modern processors use the IEEE 754 standard, which represents numbers with a fixed number of significant digits—typically 53 bits for double-precision floating-point numbers. When two numbers of vastly different magnitudes are added, the smaller number's precision may be lost entirely due to rounding. Consider adding a tiny value to a large value; the result often equals the large value because the tiny value cannot be represented within the precision budget after alignment for addition.

The order in which operations proceed directly determines which values get rounded away. If you add small numbers together first before adding them to a large number, you might accumulate enough precision to influence the final result compared to adding them one-by-one to a growing large sum. This is why (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can produce different answers when intermediate magnitudes differ substantially.

For matrix multiplication, this becomes critically important because the computation involves summing many products. A matrix-vector multiplication might involve hundreds or thousands of multiply-accumulate operations that feed into a single output value. The standard sequential reduction—where each product gets immediately added to a running sum—follows one particular order. If the computation is reorganized for parallel execution, perhaps splitting the dot product across multiple processors and later combining their results, the reduction order changes completely. This parallel reduction tree follows a different path through the arithmetic operations.

The consequences for reproducibility are substantial. Executing the same matrix multiplication with different reduction orders produces slightly different results due to different rounding patterns at each step. This is often unavoidable when distributing computation across multiple CPU cores, GPUs, or when switching between different libraries that implement reduction differently. What makes this particularly troublesome is that both results are technically correct in a floating-point sense—they both represent faithful implementations of the same mathematical operation within the bounds of floating-point error.

For scientific computing, this non-associativity creates reproducibility challenges. Researchers running the same simulation twice on different hardware, or using different numerical libraries, may obtain slightly different results in ways that are difficult to predict or control. This doesn't invalidate the results, but it complicates validation and debugging when exact numerical agreement is expected across different computational configurations.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so most real values must be rounded to the nearest representable value. In IEEE 754 double precision, a number is stored as a sign, an eleven-bit exponent, and a fifty-three-bit significand, which means each arithmetic operation returns not the exact mathematical result but that result rounded to the nearest representable neighbour. Rounding is the source of non-associativity. Consider adding a very large number, a very small number, and the negation of the large number. If the large numbers are combined first, they cancel exactly and the small number survives intact. If instead the large number and the small number are added first, the small one is shifted right during exponent alignment until its bits fall off the end of the significand; it is absorbed entirely, and the subsequent cancellation yields zero. The two orderings therefore differ by the full magnitude of the small term. Less dramatically, any sum of many terms accumulates a different pattern of rounding errors depending on the order in which partial sums are formed, because each intermediate result is rounded and that rounding error then participates in later operations. Sequential accumulation tends to lose precision once the running total grows much larger than the incoming terms, while pairwise or blocked summation keeps magnitudes comparable and usually produces smaller error, but neither is exact and neither agrees bit-for-bit with the other.

Matrix multiplication is built entirely from such sums: each output element is a dot product over the shared dimension. High-performance implementations do not evaluate that dot product in index order. They tile the computation to fit caches and registers, split the reduction dimension across threads or GPU blocks, use vector registers that maintain several independent partial sums simultaneously, and sometimes employ fused multiply-add, which rounds once rather than twice per term. Each of these choices fixes a particular reduction tree, and different choices give different trees. Consequently the same mathematical product computed with a different number of threads, a different tile size, a different vector width, a different library version, or on a different device can differ in the low-order bits. Because the atomic or nondeterministic ordering used by some parallel reductions varies from run to run, even a single binary on a single machine may not reproduce its own output exactly.

For well-conditioned problems these discrepancies are tiny, but they are amplified by ill-conditioning, by cancellation, and above all by iteration: in training a neural network or running a long simulation, a difference of one bit can grow until trajectories diverge visibly. Reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, using deterministic kernels, or adopting compensated or higher-precision accumulation, each at some cost in speed.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern computers does not obey the mathematical property of associativity, meaning that (a + b) + c does not necessarily equal a + (b + c). This fundamental limitation stems from how computers represent real numbers in binary format using a fixed number of bits, typically following the IEEE 754 standard. Each floating-point number consists of a sign bit, an exponent, and a significand or mantissa with limited precision. When two numbers of vastly different magnitudes are added, the smaller number's significant digits can be shifted beyond the precision available in the representation, causing them to be discarded entirely. This phenomenon, called catastrophic cancellation or roundoff error, means that the order in which operations are performed directly affects the final result.

Consider adding three numbers where one is much larger than the other two. If you first add the two small numbers together and then add the large number, the smaller sum might be completely lost when merged with the larger value. Conversely, if you add the large number to one small number first, then add the other small number, you may retain more precision in the intermediate steps. The hardware performs each addition with rounding at a fixed precision level, and these rounding errors accumulate differently depending on the order of operations.

Matrix multiplication exemplifies how this non-associativity becomes problematic in practice. Computing the dot product of a row and column requires summing potentially millions of floating-point products. Different reduction orders, such as summing from left to right versus using a tree-based reduction that adds partial sums in parallel, will traverse different computational paths. A sequential left-to-right summation follows a different pattern than a tree reduction that groups operations hierarchically, and both differ from other strategies that might reorder terms for vectorization or cache efficiency.

When scientists execute the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, use different compiler optimization flags, or change the number of parallel processors, the reduction order often changes subtly. A computation that ran sequentially on one machine might run in parallel on another, employing different groupings of additions. Even running identical code multiple times on the same machine can produce slightly different results if the operating system schedules threads differently.

This lack of reproducibility creates genuine challenges for scientific computing and debugging. Developers cannot simply compare numerical outputs byte-for-byte across different systems or compiler settings. Instead, they must verify results through error tolerance comparisons and statistical validation. Understanding that floating-point non-associativity is inherent to the representation, not a bug, helps researchers design robust verification strategies and communicate clearly about the numerical reliability of their computations.

Floating-point numbers are stored with a fixed number of significand bits, so most results of an arithmetic operation cannot be represented exactly and must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition itself is commutative — a + b and b + a round identically — but associativity fails because rounding happens after each individual operation, and the amount of information discarded depends on the relative magnitudes of the operands at that moment. The classic illustration in double precision is (1.0 + 1e-16) + (-1.0), where the tiny term is absorbed entirely during the first addition because aligning its exponent with 1.0 shifts its bits past the fifty-three available significand positions, leaving zero; whereas 1.0 + (1e-16 + (-1.0)) first cancels the large terms exactly, so the small quantity survives and the result is 1e-16. The same phenomenon arises whenever summands span a wide dynamic range or when catastrophic cancellation removes leading digits and promotes previously negligible rounding errors to significance. Modern hardware compounds the issue rather than causing it: fused multiply-add instructions compute a product and sum with a single rounding instead of two, extended-precision or wider internal accumulators may retain extra bits for some partial sums but not others, and vector units force sums into lane-wise partial accumulators that are combined only at the end, imposing an order dictated by register width rather than by the mathematical expression.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a large collection of dot products, each of which is a summation whose order is left unspecified by the mathematical definition. High-performance implementations exploit that freedom aggressively. They tile the operands to fit cache hierarchies, split the reduction dimension into blocks accumulated separately, unroll inner loops into several independent accumulator registers to hide instruction latency, use SIMD lanes that each hold a distinct partial sum, and on parallel machines distribute slices of the reduction across threads or GPU blocks whose partial results are merged by tree reductions or atomic updates. Every one of these choices fixes a particular parenthesization. Change the tile size, the thread count, the vector width, whether FMA contraction is enabled, or the arrival order of atomic contributions, and the parenthesization changes with it, so the computed entries differ in their last few bits even though the same inputs and the same nominal algorithm were used.

Consequently, results are not bitwise reproducible across libraries, hardware generations, compiler flags, or even repeated runs of the same nondeterministic kernel. For well-conditioned problems the discrepancies stay near machine epsilon times the magnitude of the intermediate terms and are harmless. They become consequential when downstream logic amplifies them: iterative solvers may take different numbers of steps, comparisons and branches may flip, ill-conditioned or heavily cancelling computations may lose many digits, and long training runs may diverge visibly. Remedies include enforcing a fixed reduction order, using deterministic library modes, compensated or higher-precision accumulation, or accepting the variation and validating results against error bounds rather than exact bit patterns.

Reproducibility becomes essential in scientific applications where results must be validated or audited. Some projects address this through techniques like using higher precision for intermediate calculations, implementing deterministic reduction orders at the cost of parallelism, or accepting reproducibility only within statistical bounds. This fundamental departure from pure mathematics arises directly from how floating-point numbers are represented and manipulated in hardware.

Modern computers represent floating-point numbers using a fixed number of bits to encode a sign, an exponent, and a mantissa or significand. This finite precision means that not all real numbers can be represented exactly, and many arithmetic operations must be rounded to fit within these constraints. When adding two floating-point numbers, the hardware must first align their exponents, add the mantissas, and then round the result to the nearest representable value. This rounding step is where associativity breaks down.

Consider adding three numbers where intermediate results require rounding. If we compute (a + b) + c, the sum a + b might round to some value that, when added to c, produces a different result than computing a + (b + c), where b + c rounds first and then combines with a. The discrepancy occurs because rounding a different intermediate sum can compound errors in unexpected ways. Additionally, the magnitude of numbers matters significantly in floating-point arithmetic. Adding a very large number to a very small number can cause the small number's contribution to be entirely lost due to the limited precision of the mantissa. The order in which we add values therefore directly affects which information gets preserved and which gets discarded.

This issue becomes critical when performing large matrix multiplications, where we must sum many products together to compute a single element of the result matrix. Different reduction orders—different sequences in which we accumulate the partial products—lead to accumulating rounding errors differently. Sequential execution on a CPU produces yet another result. For scientific applications requiring bit-for-bit reproducibility, this presents a genuine challenge: the same matrix multiplication can produce slightly different answers depending on how the computation is parallelized or which hardware executes it.

Modern solutions include using higher-precision accumulation, implementing reproducible summation algorithms that enforce fixed reduction orders, or using decimal arithmetic where available, each representing different trade-offs between accuracy, performance, and reproducibility.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity in Matrix Multiplication

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware deviates fundamentally from the mathematical properties we expect from real numbers. While addition of real numbers is associative—meaning that (a + b) + c always equals a + (b + c)—floating-point addition decidedly is not. This deviation arises from the finite precision inherent in how computers represent numbers using binary formats like IEEE 754 double precision.

When two floating-point numbers are added, the result is rounded to fit within the available precision. The rounding error introduced depends on the magnitudes of the operands and their sum. Critically, when three numbers are combined, the order in which we pair them for addition affects which intermediate values get rounded, leading to different final results. For instance, adding a very large number to a very small number and then adding a medium number might lose the small number entirely due to rounding, whereas a different pairing might preserve more information. The order of operations thus determines which rounding errors accumulate.

This non-associativity becomes particularly problematic in matrix multiplication, a fundamental operation in scientific computing. Computing a single element of the result matrix requires accumulating the product of many pairs of numbers from the input matrices. If we reduce these products in different orders, we obtain different results. In simple terms, computing the dot product of two vectors by summing left-to-right produces a different answer than summing right-to-left, and both differ from other reduction orders.

When matrix multiplications are executed on different hardware architectures or using different libraries, the reduction order frequently differs. A GPU might process elements in parallel with a specific reduction tree structure, while a CPU implementation might accumulate results sequentially in a different order. Even across different versions of the same library, algorithmic improvements or compiler optimizations might alter the order in which operations execute.

This variability directly threatens reproducibility in scientific computing. Large simulations that depend on matrix multiplication—from machine learning training to climate modeling—can produce noticeably different results when run on different systems or even when run multiple times if multithreaded implementations use non-deterministic scheduling. The numerical differences might be small for individual operations but accumulate significantly across thousands or millions of matrix multiplications in a simulation.

Researchers and practitioners address this challenge through reproducible reduction algorithms that enforce a consistent order of operations, sacrificing some performance for deterministic results. Alternatively, some accept the irreproducibility as inherent to the hardware while employing statistical methods to validate results. Understanding floating-point non-associativity thus remains essential for anyone requiring reliable numerical computations at scale.

If intermediate sums have magnitudes that differ significantly, smaller values effectively disappear during alignment, as their least significant bits shift beyond the precision boundary and are truncated. The order in which we combine numbers therefore determines which bits are discarded and which are preserved.

Then adding the medium number gives one result. This is not a bug but an inherent property of fixed-precision arithmetic.

An identical mathematical operation can produce results that differ in the last few significant digits when executed with different reduction orderings. Consider adding one, then a very small quantity such as 10^-20, then the negative of one. If the small quantity is added to one first, the exact sum falls between two representable neighbours of one, and rounding discards it entirely; subtracting one afterwards yields exactly zero. If instead one and its negative are combined first, the result is exactly zero, and adding the small quantity preserves it in full. Same operands, same operator, two different answers, differing not in the last bit but by the entire magnitude of the small term. The general phenomenon is that summing numbers of widely varying magnitudes loses the low-order bits of the small ones, and how much is lost depends on the order in which partial sums accumulate. Cancellation between nearly equal quantities magnifies whatever error has already crept in, so the discrepancy between orderings can be arbitrarily large in the worst case, though in practice it is usually near the level of accumulated rounding noise.

Matrix multiplication is built almost entirely from long summations: every output element is a dot product, a reduction over the shared dimension. Nothing in the definition of the product specifies the order in which those terms are added, and high-performance implementations exploit that freedom aggressively. They tile the computation to fit caches, split the reduction dimension across many threads or GPU blocks and combine partial results in a tree, use vector registers that accumulate four or eight or sixteen independent partial sums in parallel lanes, and sometimes employ fused multiply-add instructions that round once instead of twice. Each of these choices imposes a particular grouping of the additions, and because addition is not associative, each grouping can produce a different bit pattern for the same mathematical result.

The practical consequence is that the same matrices multiplied on the same machine may give different answers when the thread count changes, when a library selects a different kernel because the shapes or alignment differ, when work is scheduled dynamically so that partial sums arrive in a nondeterministic order, or when the code is moved to different hardware. All the answers are usually equally accurate, none is uniquely correct, but they are not identical, which frustrates bitwise-reproducible testing, complicates debugging of iterative algorithms where tiny differences amplify, and explains why deterministic modes in numerical libraries exist and why they cost performance.

If we instead compute a + (b + c), we round b + c first, then add a to that rounded result and round again. Because the intermediate rounding happens at different points and to different intermediate quantities, the two final results can differ, even though real-number addition is perfectly associative. The magnitude of the discrepancy depends on the relative sizes and signs of the operands: adding numbers of very different magnitudes, or subtracting nearly equal quantities, tends to amplify the rounding error, so the choice of order can matter a great deal in practice, not just in principle.

This has direct consequences for large matrix multiplications, where each output element is computed as a sum of many products, effectively a long reduction over the shared dimension. Mathematically the reduction order is irrelevant, but on real hardware it is not. Modern accelerators such as GPUs and multi-core CPUs parallelize these reductions across threads, cores, or vector lanes, and use techniques like tree reductions, blocked or tiled accumulation, and hardware fused multiply-add units. The order in which partial sums are combined depends on the number of threads, the tile size, the scheduling, and even runtime conditions such as which core finishes first in a nondeterministic race. Different libraries, different hardware generations, different thread counts, or even different runs of the same program on the same hardware can therefore produce summations that are grouped differently, and because floating-point addition is not associative, this yields slightly different final results for the same mathematical matrix product.

For a single dot product the differences are usually at the level of the last bit or two of precision, but in large-scale computations these small discrepancies can accumulate or be amplified through subsequent operations, especially in iterative algorithms like neural network training or numerical solvers, where results feed back into further computations. This makes bitwise reproducibility across different hardware, different parallelization strategies, or even different runs a genuine challenge, and it is why frameworks that require strict determinism must fix the reduction order explicitly, often at some cost to performance, rather than relying on the mathematical equivalence of different summation orders.

# Floating-Point Addition and Non-Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern computers represents numbers using a fixed number of bits to encode the significand and exponent, following standards like IEEE 754. This finite precision creates a fundamental limitation: when two numbers differ greatly in magnitude, adding them causes information loss. The smaller number's digits may fall below the precision threshold of the larger number, becoming effectively invisible during addition.

Consider adding three numbers where the magnitude gap is significant. If you first add two large numbers and then add a small number to their sum, the small number might be rounded away entirely. Conversely, if you add the small number to one of the large numbers first, you still lose precision, but you might lose different bits. The mathematical property of associativity—that (a + b) + c should equal a + (b + c)—simply does not hold in floating-point arithmetic. The order of operations genuinely produces different results, and both are technically correct within the limitations of the representation.

This non-associativity becomes profoundly problematic in large matrix multiplications, where reproducibility is critical for scientific computing, machine learning, and numerical simulations. When multiplying two large matrices, each element of the result requires summing many products. Computing a single result element involves accumulating perhaps thousands of individual floating-point multiplications. The order in which these products are added together directly affects the final result due to the non-associativity problem.

Different computational approaches will naturally sum these products in different orders. A sequential algorithm that processes products left to right produces different accumulated rounding errors than a parallel algorithm that divides work across multiple processors and combines partial sums in a tree-like reduction pattern. Even running identical code on different hardware or with different compiler optimization levels can change the reduction order and thus change the result. Some compilers might unroll loops differently, some processors might execute instructions in unexpected orders due to pipelining, and different parallelization strategies will definitely change the associativity structure.

This means that reproducing numerical results from matrix multiplications becomes nearly impossible without careful control over the exact computation sequence. Scientists cannot reliably verify results from colleagues using different hardware or software configurations. Machine learning models trained with different parallelization strategies produce different weights, potentially undermining the reproducibility crisis already affecting computational science.

Addressing this requires either accepting non-reproducibility as inherent to the computational approach, using higher precision arithmetic at the cost of performance, or employing specialized reduction algorithms designed to minimize error accumulation in specific orders. Understanding this limitation is essential for anyone working with numerical computation at scale.

Whether that loss happens depends on what the operand magnitudes are at the moment of the addition, and those magnitudes depend on which partial sums have already been accumulated. A canonical illustration is adding 1.0, then a tiny value like 2⁻⁶⁰, then −1.0. Grouping as (1.0 + 2⁻⁶⁰) − 1.0 gives exactly zero, because the tiny value is entirely absorbed by rounding into the representation of 1.0. Grouping as 1.0 + (2⁻⁶⁰ − 1.0) preserves the tiny contribution, yielding 2⁻⁶⁰. The two orderings differ by the full magnitude of one of the operands. More generally, each addition can introduce a relative error of about one unit in the last place, and the way those errors accumulate — whether they cancel, compound, or get swamped — is a function of the summation order. Catastrophic cancellation, where two nearly equal quantities are subtracted and the leading digits annihilate, amplifies whatever rounding noise was present in the operands, so the sensitivity to ordering can be far larger than a naive error bound suggests.

This matters for matrix multiplication because every output element is a dot product, that is, a sum of many products, and the reduction over the contraction index can be organized in countless ways. A blocked or tiled implementation sums within tiles first and then combines tile results, which is a different association than a straightforward sequential loop. Multithreaded implementations split the reduction across cores and combine partial sums in an order that may depend on scheduling, thread count, or the order in which threads finish. Vectorized kernels maintain several independent accumulators, one per SIMD lane, and merge them at the end, again changing the grouping. GPUs add tree reductions across warps and blocks, sometimes with atomic accumulation whose order is genuinely nondeterministic from run to run. Libraries also select among multiple kernel variants based on matrix shape, alignment, and available instruction sets, and some hardware offers fused multiply-add or extended-precision internal accumulators that change rounding behavior relative to separate multiply and add steps.

The consequence is that the same mathematical product computed on different machines, with different thread counts, different library versions, or even different runs of the same nondeterministic kernel, can yield results that differ in the last few bits. Those differences are usually small in a relative sense, but they are not zero, and in iterative or chaotic computations they can grow. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, using deterministic kernels, or employing compensated or exactly-rounded summation algorithms, all of which cost performance.

This rounding behavior depends on the relative magnitudes and signs of the operands at the moment the addition is performed, not just on the mathematical values being combined. Consequently, the order in which a sequence of numbers is summed can change the intermediate magnitudes involved at each step, which changes where and how much rounding occurs, and ultimately changes the final result. This is why (a + b) + c is not guaranteed to equal a + (b + c) in floating-point arithmetic, even though the two expressions are mathematically identical over the real numbers.

This lack of associativity becomes especially significant in large matrix multiplications, where each output element is computed as a sum of many products, often thousands or millions in deep learning workloads. On modern hardware, this summation is rarely performed as a single sequential accumulation. Instead, the work is distributed across many parallel processing units, such as GPU cores or vectorized SIMD lanes, and partial sums are computed independently before being combined. The specific grouping and order of these partial sums depends on hardware-specific factors such as tile sizes, thread scheduling, the number of parallel execution units, memory access patterns, and even runtime conditions that can vary between executions. Because different hardware architectures, different libraries, or even different runs on the same hardware can produce different reduction orders, the accumulated rounding errors differ as well, leading to results that are numerically close but not bit-for-bit identical.

This has direct practical consequences for reproducibility. Two runs of the same matrix multiplication algorithm on different GPUs, or even the same GPU with different batch sizes or thread configurations, can yield slightly different numerical results despite implementing the same mathematical operation. In most contexts these differences are negligible, but in settings requiring strict reproducibility, such as scientific computing, regulatory verification, or debugging subtle training instabilities in machine learning models, these small discrepancies can compound over many operations, especially in iterative processes like neural network training, making exact bitwise reproducibility across hardware or software versions difficult to guarantee without deliberately fixing the reduction order.

This shifting can push low-order bits of the smaller number beyond the precision the format can hold, causing them to be rounded off. Consequently, the result of a floating-point addition is not the true mathematical sum but the nearest representable number to it. Because the rounding error introduced depends on the relative magnitudes and signs of the operands being combined at each step, changing the order in which numbers are added changes which values get rounded and by how much. So while real-number addition satisfies (a+b)+c = a+(b+c), floating-point addition may not, since intermediate rounding can differ depending on the grouping.

This has direct consequences for large matrix multiplications, which are essentially collections of long dot products—sums of many products accumulated together. The final value of each output element depends on the order in which the individual products are summed. On modern hardware, this order is rarely fixed: it can be influenced by how a compiler vectorizes the loop, how a GPU or multicore CPU splits the reduction across threads or SIMD lanes, whether the operations are fused (as in fused multiply-add instructions), and how libraries like BLAS partition the workload into tiles or blocks for cache efficiency. Different hardware architectures, different thread counts, or even different runs on the same machine with dynamic scheduling can produce different reduction orders. Since each distinct order accumulates rounding errors differently, the bitwise result of a matrix multiplication can vary slightly from run to run or from platform to platform, even though the mathematical operation being performed is identical.

For many applications this variability is harmless, since the differences are on the order of machine epsilon and do not affect the qualitative correctness of results. But in contexts requiring strict reproducibility—such as verifying scientific computations, debugging numerical pipelines, or ensuring deterministic behavior in machine learning training across different GPUs—these small discrepancies can accumulate over many operations, especially in deep neural networks with millions of matrix multiplications chained together, leading to divergent results despite identical inputs and algorithms. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, using specialized deterministic algorithms, or employing higher-precision or compensated summation techniques, all of which typically come at some cost in performance or hardware flexibility.

The IEEE 754 standard defines how processors represent and manipulate numbers using a fixed number of bits, typically 64 bits for double precision. This limitation means that not all real numbers can be represented exactly, and operations produce results rounded to the nearest representable value.

Specifically, when a number much larger than another is added to it, the smaller number's least significant bits may be discarded during rounding, causing permanent loss of precision. The order in which numbers are combined therefore affects which information gets lost.

This non-associativity becomes critically important in matrix multiplication, particularly when processing large matrices on distributed computing systems or with different algorithmic approaches. Matrix multiplication fundamentally involves computing dot products—the sum of many element-wise products. When different hardware configurations or software implementations process the same matrix multiplication with different reduction orders, they produce numerically different results. One implementation might sum partial products from left to right, while another sums from right to left, or uses a tree-based reduction scheme that groups operations hierarchically. Each approach accumulates floating-point error differently, leading to results that diverge in their least significant bits.

This becomes especially problematic for reproducibility in scientific computing. Running the same matrix multiplication twice on different processors, or with different numbers of parallel threads, can produce slightly different answers because the summation order changes. This inconsistency complicates validation, debugging, and compliance in fields where reproducible results are essential.

Researchers have developed strategies to address this issue, such as using higher precision intermediate calculations, employing error-correction techniques, or enforcing strict summation orders. However, these solutions typically incur performance penalties. The fundamental tension remains: optimizing for speed often means reordering operations in ways that violate associativity, while maintaining reproducibility requires sacrificing efficient parallelization strategies. Understanding this limitation is crucial for anyone working with large-scale numerical computations where both performance and precision matter.

When two numbers of vastly different magnitudes are added, the smaller number's digits may be entirely lost during the alignment phase of addition, a phenomenon called catastrophic cancellation. The order in which operands are combined therefore determines which information gets discarded, leading to different results.

Consider a practical example: adding a very large number, a moderate number, and a very small number. If we first add the large and small numbers, the small number disappears entirely and we have merely the large number. Adding the moderate number then yields one result. Conversely, if we add the moderate and small numbers first, we preserve their combined contribution before merging with the large number, potentially preserving more precision in the final answer. Neither order is inherently "correct" in the floating-point sense—they simply compute different things.

This nonassociativity becomes critically important in matrix multiplication at scale. The number of possible reduction orders for summing a column of products grows combinatorially with the vector length. Different processors, different compiler optimizations, and different algorithm implementations naturally choose different reduction orders. A GPU might process partial sums in parallel using a tree-reduction strategy, while a CPU processes elements sequentially from left to right. These choices are computationally efficient but produce slightly different numerical results.

For reproducibility, this is deeply problematic. Two implementations of the same matrix multiplication that differ only in their reduction order—perhaps one using row-major and another using column-major layout, or one parallelized differently than another—will produce results that diverge in their least significant digits. With cascading errors through multiple matrix multiplications, as occurs in deep neural networks or iterative numerical solvers, these small differences can grow to become large discrepancies.

Achieving reproducible results across different hardware and software configurations requires either accepting these differences as inherent to floating-point computation, or explicitly controlling the reduction order through software mechanisms that sacrifice some performance for deterministic results. The tension between numerical efficiency and reproducibility remains a fundamental challenge in scientific computing.

Since floating-point addition is not associative, different reduction orders produce results that differ in their low-order bits, and these tiny discrepancies can propagate and amplify through subsequent layers of computation, especially in deep neural networks or iterative numerical algorithms.

The practical consequence is that running the same matrix multiplication on different hardware, different thread counts, or different library versions can yield numerically distinct results, even though all computations are performed correctly according to floating-point rules. This makes bit-for-bit reproducibility difficult to guarantee across platforms, complicates debugging and testing, and requires researchers to rely on tolerance-based comparisons or deterministic reduction algorithms when exact reproducibility is required for scientific or regulatory purposes.

# Floating-Point Addition and Associativity

Floating-point arithmetic on modern hardware operates under the IEEE 754 standard, which represents numbers with finite precision using a fixed number of bits for the mantissa and exponent. This constraint fundamentally breaks the mathematical property of associativity for addition, meaning that (a + b) + c does not necessarily equal a + (b + c) when computed on actual hardware.

The root cause lies in rounding. When two floating-point numbers are added, the result must be rounded to fit within the available precision. Consider adding three numbers where the intermediate results differ based on grouping. If we compute (a + b) first and then add c, we perform one rounding after the first addition and another after the second. If instead we compute (a + c) first and then add b, the intermediate result differs, triggering different rounding behavior and potentially producing a different final answer. The rounding errors accumulate and propagate differently depending on the order of operations.

A concrete example illustrates this: adding a very large number to a very small number can cause the small number's contribution to be lost entirely if the large number dominates the mantissa. The position of this operation in a sequence of additions determines how much information is preserved. If we add multiple small numbers together first before combining with a large number, we might accumulate enough precision to survive the final addition. If we add the large number earlier, individual small numbers disappear into rounding error.

Matrix multiplication amplifies this problem significantly. A standard matrix multiplication involves computing dot products, where each element is the sum of many products. The order in which these products are accumulated determines the final result. Different reduction orders—such as processing rows before columns, or varying how parallel threads accumulate partial sums—produce different intermediate values and thus different rounding patterns.

For large matrices, this non-associativity becomes practically significant. When the same multiplication is performed with different reduction orders, perhaps due to varying numbers of parallel processors or different algorithmic implementations, the results diverge. The deviations grow with matrix size because larger matrices involve more terms being summed, compounding rounding errors. What might be a difference in the fifteenth decimal place for small matrices can become differences in earlier decimal places for very large computations.

This non-associativity creates reproducibility challenges in scientific computing. Identical algorithms running on different hardware configurations, or even the same hardware with different thread scheduling, produce slightly different answers. For many applications this variation is negligible, but in iterative solvers, machine learning training, or sensitivity analyses where small differences compound, achieving bit-identical reproducibility across different execution orders is impossible without implementing special mitigation strategies like fixed reduction orders or extended precision accumulators.

Floating-point numbers occupy a finite number of bits, so each arithmetic result must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition itself is exact in the sense that the true sum of two representable numbers is computed and then rounded once, but that rounding step is where associativity breaks. Consider three numbers a, b, and c. When we compute (a+b)+c, the intermediate sum a+b is rounded before c is added, and the rounded intermediate discards information that would have influenced the final result had c been incorporated first. Computing a+(b+c) rounds a different intermediate, discards different information, and therefore can produce a different final answer. The classic illustration uses a very large number, a very small number, and the negation of the large number: adding the large pair first annihilates them and leaves the small value intact, while adding the small value to the large one first causes it to vanish entirely into the rounding, leaving zero. The discrepancy is not a bug but a direct consequence of finite precision, and it means that the order in which a long chain of additions is performed genuinely changes the computed sum.

Matrix multiplication is essentially a vast collection of dot products, each of which is a sum of many products. On modern hardware there is enormous pressure to reorder those sums. Vector instructions accumulate several partial sums in parallel lanes and combine them at the end. Multiple threads or GPU warps split a long dot product into chunks, sum each chunk independently, and then reduce the partial results in whatever order they happen to finish. Cache blocking and tiling algorithms subdivide the matrices so that contributions to a single output element arrive in a sequence dictated by memory layout rather than by index order. Fused multiply-add instructions retain extra precision in the product before adding, changing the rounding pattern relative to a separate multiply and add. Atomic accumulation across threads introduces nondeterministic ordering that can vary from run to run even on identical hardware with identical inputs.

The practical consequence is that the same mathematical matrix product, computed by two different libraries, on two different numbers of threads, on two different GPU models, or with two different tile sizes, will generally yield results that differ in the last few bits. Those tiny differences can amplify through subsequent operations, so that iterative solvers converge in different numbers of steps, ill-conditioned problems produce visibly different answers, and machine learning training runs diverge into different models. Achieving bitwise reproducibility therefore requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, using deterministic accumulation schemes, or employing compensated or extended-precision summation, all of which sacrifice some performance in exchange for repeatable output.

Floating-point numbers are stored with a fixed number of significand bits, so most real results of an arithmetic operation cannot be represented exactly and must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition of two floating-point numbers is therefore not the true mathematical sum but the correctly rounded version of it, and that rounding step is what destroys associativity. When you compute (a + b) + c, the intermediate a + b is rounded before c is added, and information that fell below the precision of the intermediate result is lost permanently; computing a + (b + c) discards a different set of low-order bits. A classic illustration in double precision is adding one, then 10⁻²⁰, then minus one: grouping the first two together yields exactly one, because 10⁻²⁰ is far below the roughly 10⁻¹⁶ relative spacing near one, so the final result is zero, while grouping the last two together preserves the tiny term and yields 10⁻²⁰. Catastrophic cancellation, in which nearby large values subtract to leave a small result dominated by earlier rounding error, magnifies these discrepancies, and overflow or underflow can make the ordering matter even more dramatically, turning a finite answer into an infinity or a zero.

Matrix multiplication is a dense collection of dot products, each a long summation, so every element of the output depends on a chosen reduction order. High-performance implementations do not sum in the naive left-to-right order. They tile the computation to fit caches, split the contraction dimension across threads, GPU warps, or separate nodes, accumulate partial sums in vector registers with several independent accumulators so that the hardware's pipelined adders stay busy, and then combine those partial sums in a tree. Fused multiply-add instructions add a further wrinkle, since they round once instead of twice. All of these choices are legitimate and all give results that are accurate to within the expected error bound, but they give different bit patterns. Consequently the same library on the same machine can return different answers when the number of threads changes, when a different tile size or kernel is selected for a different matrix shape, when work is distributed differently across a cluster, or when a new hardware generation offers wider vectors or different accumulation precision.

The practical consequence is that bitwise reproducibility must be engineered rather than assumed. Small differences amplify through iterative solvers, training loops, and branch conditions, so two runs can diverge visibly even though both are correct. Remedies include fixing the reduction order deterministically, using deterministic library modes, employing compensated or extended-precision accumulation, or exact fixed-point accumulators, each trading some performance for repeatability.

Floating-point numbers are stored with a finite number of significand bits, so most results of arithmetic operations cannot be represented exactly and must be rounded to the nearest representable value. Addition of two floats therefore returns not their true sum but the rounded sum, and the size of that rounding error depends on the magnitude of the result: the spacing between adjacent representable numbers grows with the exponent. Consequently, when three numbers are added, the intermediate value produced first determines how much precision is available for the second addition, and different groupings produce different intermediate magnitudes. A classic illustration is adding a very large number, its negation, and a small number. If the large pair is combined first, they cancel exactly and the small value survives; if the large number is combined with the small one first, the small contribution is swallowed because it falls below the last representable bit at that magnitude, and the subsequent cancellation yields zero. The two groupings give different answers, so the operation is not associative. Similar effects arise without exact cancellation whenever the terms differ substantially in scale, and even among terms of similar scale the accumulated rounding differs slightly between orderings. Note that addition remains commutative, since swapping the operands of a single addition does not change the rounded result; it is only the grouping that matters. Hardware features can accentuate or hide the discrepancy, for instance fused multiply-add operations that round once instead of twice, extended-precision accumulators, and the fact that different instruction sequences may keep intermediate values in registers of differing width.

Matrix multiplication is built from dot products, each of which is a sum of many products, so its result depends on the order in which those partial sums are combined. High-performance implementations do not evaluate the sum in the naive left-to-right order. They tile the computation to fit caches, split the summation dimension into blocks handled by separate threads or separate GPU warps, use vector registers that maintain several independent partial accumulators simultaneously, and finish with a tree-shaped combination of those partials. The particular decomposition chosen depends on the matrix dimensions, the tile sizes selected by autotuning, the number of threads available, the presence or absence of fused multiply-add, and even the nondeterministic order in which atomic updates from concurrent workers arrive at a shared accumulator. Every one of these choices alters the grouping of additions and therefore the low-order bits of the answer.

The practical consequence is that the same mathematical product computed on two machines, with two library versions, with a different thread count, or twice on the same GPU with atomics, can differ in the final bits. Those small differences amplify through iterative algorithms, through comparisons near decision boundaries, and through long training runs, so bitwise reproducibility requires deliberately fixing the reduction order, disabling atomics and autotuning, or using compensated or higher-precision accumulation, generally at some cost in speed.
